projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Vincent Ciccone was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Good morning. My name is Paul J. Frisco, and I am the interview coordinator for the Center for World War II Studies and Conflict Resolution here on the campus of Brookdale Community College at Lincroft, New Jersey. This morning we are privileged to have with us Mr. Vincent Ciccone, whose military career was spent with the Air Corps, the Army Air Corps. And I'm going to let you start out by first telling us where were you when the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay. At that time I was living in Brooklyn, okay? And that was December 7, 1941. We heard about the attack on Pearl Harbor, and we were waiting for President Roosevelt to get on the air that Sunday morning. And he was a terrific orator. In fact, he was known for his fireside chats, you know? And he came on the air and he told us what had happened, that the Empire of Japan had committed a sneak, unprovoked, dastardly attack on Pearl Harbor. And that that day would go down in infamy. And then he told us, you know, what had happened over there, the damage that was done. And over there we didn't have TV in those days, so all we would listen. We never saw videos except if we went to a movie on a weekend and they had--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Newsreels.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Newsreels, Fox Movietone News, you know? That's it. You had visual effects. But sometimes your imagination played, you know. It would give you more of a feeling for what was happening than actual videos.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: How old were you, and how did you feel when you heard about that?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, at that time I was 17. I was sitting on the floor and just lookingup at the radio and listening to President Roosevelt. How did I feel? Well, you know, the war was going on in Europe, you know, with Hitler invading all those countries and with those buzz bombs going over to Great Britain and all the damage they were doing, and we heard about that and what was going on. And we weren'tinvolved in it, although we were sending in a lot of supplies to help out Britain.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I'm sorry. Did you rush to a recruitment office to sign up?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I was too young. I was 17 at the time. I was in my last year of high school. But as soon as I turned 18 in November, I went to the recruitment center in New York, December the 11th or 12, I forget the exact date, and I took all the preliminary tests to become an aviation cadet, and I passed all the tests. And I was going out for a navigator because I was good at math, physics, and celestial navigation. That's what I wanted. And I passed all the tests, and they waited till I graduated, and they called me in on February 22 of 1943. And then we had that supreme war effort going on, you know, with the whole nation uniting, defense plants, and all the women working in defense plants. Rosie the Riveter, you heard of that, right? And all the able-bodied men going into service. Most people don't know that there was 11 million people in service. 11 million.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Can I correct you?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Go ahead. How many?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: The final number was 16 million.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: 16 million?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: 16 million. Only reason I'm telling you that, we found out yesterday.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay. How about casualties? How many? 400,000?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Over a million.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, that's all over the world, but not American casualties.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: American casualties, now you're putting me on the spot.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, I know that. I understand it was 400,000.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Well, I think there were 450,000 that may have been killed.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: And almost that number that were wounded.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Don't hold me to it. I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's all right. Actually, it was aworld war. There was millions killed all over the world, you know? All right, so we were at what point?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: You were--you passed all your tests.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: And where were you? Where did they send you for your basic training?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I went to Atlantic City. Now you know--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That had to be hard to take.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, what do you mean? It was deserted. We took over the hotels, and it was freezing cold. We were working out on the beach, you know, drilling, and I wore every piece of cloth that they gave me to keep warm it was so cold.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Was this at the Berkeley Carteret?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No. I was at the Hotel Dennis on the fifth floor overlooking the ocean, okay? Fifth floor. We took over that place, and most of it was all indoctrination. You had to see movies about what to expect and everything like that. And from there, you know with the Army you get on a troop train, you never knew where you were going. It was always a surprise, okay? And from there where were we going? Theysent us to college, Amherst State College in Massachusetts. We had our own dormitory with the regular college students. It was nice. It was a good period of my life. We went to the cafeterias with them and everything. Although we didn't have to pay.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: What did you do, bunk two to a room in the dormitories?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: You know, I don't remember that fact.But we all bunked together.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: But you lived on the campus.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We lived on the campus in our own dormitory, and we participated with everything there. And we had mostly math, physics, trigonometry, advanced algebra and all that, but I went to parochial high school, and it was--I didn't have to--all I did was sit back and just help out the guys.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I'm sorry. At that point did you know what assignment would be yours, you know--

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Where I was going to be assigned, no,because from that point after we left the college, we went down to Nashville, Tennessee. It was a classification center where they gave you all kinds of tests. All kind of aptitude tests, physical tests and everything like that. This is where they classify you, right? So I wanted navigating. I wanted to navigate that bomber and bring it back home. So I passed all the tests and they were short of pilots, and they said, "We need pilots, you're a pilot." "I'm a pilot." So we went through all pre-flight training and all of that, and the first primary training when I first started to fly was in--it was in Albany, Georgia where the government took over a private flying school. It was called Darr Aero Tech, D-a double r. And we were taught by civilian instructors, okay? Now, when these guys taught you, they taught you under pressure, okay? They made me dislike flying. These instructors cursed you out; they made you feel so small.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: They were motivating you.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Motivating, no way. They were killing you. I had to learn under pressure. I had to be quick, fast, that's all. Otherwise, get away. "We need you guys, we got to get up there, we need pilots, okay?" And so I first started flying, we were flying PT Stearmans, bi-wing airplane, open cockpit, two guys. The instructor was in front and the student was in the back. And after the first flight, we called it the bucket brigade. We had to get pails of water and wash off the sides of the plane because they put you through the mill. Everything had to be fast, you know. These planes were aerobatic. They could stall, spins, everything like that, you know. And I saw after 10, 12 hours and this guy, he was a Russian guy, Gastevo. I remember his name. I hated him. I'm sorry to say that, but he just made me dislike flying. You had to fly every day. I just didn't want to fly with him. I went to the commandant of cadets and I says, "Look," I says, "I didn't want this, you know, and I wanted navigation." I said, "You got me doing this. I dislike what I'm doing." He gave me the old spiel, "Well, a lot of us are doing jobs which we don't like, but you got to do it. It's for the country. You got to do it." So I hung on, and I went to see him again, and he wouldn't transfer me to navigation school. And when I took a check ride by a flight officer, I think it had to be maybe about after I had 50 hours, and I told him how I felt about it, and instinctively I was flying because I couldn't help--you know, you do things instinctively. But I passed the tests. But I told him how I felt, and he worked it out with the commandant and they transferred me. Not to navigation, because I don't think the commandant liked me. They sent me to aerial gunnery school in Lowrey, California. Which I happened to like. I had a lot of fun there. Learned all about weapons. And--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Before we get into that--

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We didn't even get to the war yet.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: We'll get you there.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So you now had two long train rides.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Was there anything that stands out inyour mind today about those rides on the train that took so long?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: On the train? Yeah. I went from the south, I went to Denver, Colorado and I went to--I had special orders so I went-- it wasn't on a troop train. It was on a regular train.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So you were lucky.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah. I had special assignments. I went to Denver, Colorado, and it was in the wintertime, Lowry Air Force Base, and it was freezing. Again, I put on every piece of clothing that I had to go to sleep in that cold freezing--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That was just building up.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah. But I had good times there. We made a lot of friends and I enjoyed the training and everything. We were trained with these .50 caliber Browning machine guns, okay? The shells were about that long, half an inch. They called them .50 calibers. When you heard one of them going off, you couldn't believe it. The sound of that, whoo.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Okay. Now we're going to get you into the war. When you went all through this training. You went through that period where they were trying to make you a pilot and you didn't want to be and you finally got near your wish, however, you didn't get to be a navigator. They made you a gunner.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: When did they assign you to an air group and send you overseas?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I wasn't assigned to an air group. I was assigned to a pilot. It was just a pilot and me. And his name was Junior. Junior Smeltzer. In fact, he's in the picture, one of these pictures here, Junior Smeltzer.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: You want to show it?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: He was all of 22 and I was 19, so we made a good team. And that's Juniorsitting down there. And that was part of our ground crew. And we made a terrific team because he was just as gung ho as I was, you know? And we--that came out good. And we did our overseas training over Myrtle Beach. You know the beach at Myrtle Beach? We did strafing on the ground, and we had tow planes, towed targets, and we were practicing gunnery training, how youlead a target while you were moving in the air. All kinds of training like that. We did our overseas training, and we were a team, Junior and I, okay? And we went overseas as a replacement. We went over to New Guinea, andwe were a replacement for the 417th Bomb Group.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I'm curious about that trip from the States to New Guinea. How did you make that, by flying or by ship?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We flew by a C-54. That's a heavy cargo plane. We didn't make it all the way. We stopped in Honolulu and then some other island, Canary Island, then New Guinea. We didn't know where we were going. They never tell you what you're doing, where you're going to go. It's a surprise. "Oh, New Guinea." At that time we were on the western part of the island. There was Port Moresby and Nadzab, and the rest of the island was cut off. The Japs were on the rest of the island, the eastern part of the island. And as soon as we walked in the camp, everybody was hollering, "Oh, first blood, new blood, here we come." Yeah, they're very excited, you know? So the first mission that we were assigned to, they called it a milk run, an easy run, no opposition. So what we did was we had--we flew over the eastern part of the island, okay? Now, we took off, we were treetop level, okay? And so they couldn't hear us. We came up on them, and that was my first baptism of fire. When that happened, the adrenalin starts to flow and they're in the water and on the beach and eh-eh-eh-eh-eh. And we just shoot. They just ran into the jungle, into the woods. That was my first mission, and that stands out in my mind. Jonathan Lewis(Second questioner/Freehold Township High School student): So going back a step, when you stopped in Honolulu to refill the gas tanks of the plane, did you see Pearl Harbor when you were there?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No. No. We just--you know, it was just a stopover in Honolulu to refuel and that was it. But I saw nothing of Pearl Harbor and what remained of what happened, no. I didn't see any of that.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So you completed your first so-called "milk run."

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Milk run.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: And how did you feel when you landed after the action?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, after the action, you know, you get debriefed, but prior to that we were briefed, we went to Intelligence. They brief you to where you're going, what you're going to do, what to expect to see, all that and everything like that. When you come back from a mission, you're debriefed and you tell them what you saw and everything. And when you're all done, they give you a two-ounce shot of whiskey, and that helped because your ears were ringing and you were, whew, made it back, okay?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Now, your crew consisted of how many?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Just us, just Junior and I.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Just the two of you. That was the crew.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah. If you look at this picture--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Is that the plane?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah. That's the plane. That's it. It's the A-20. It has four 50s in the nose and a gun turret with two 50s on top. So it was just the pilot and I. We had a small bomb bay. We carried small bombs. Are you interested in the type of bombs that we carried?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I don't think you have to go into that detail. I'd rather have you tell about your actions--

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: --and what life was like in New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, we had jungle training. That'sabout it. I only flew that one mission in New Guinea. Then we moved up to the Dutch East Indies. That was a series of islands. We were on one island called Numfor, because from there we were on mission. We were on the lower islands of the Philippines, like Leyte, Mindanao, and Mindoro, those islands there. We were concentrating on that. Most of our missions were in support of ground troops. We'd--when we supported them, they would, like, shoot a smoke bomb into the area that we would have to concentrate on, and we'd come down treetop level strafing. And depending on the type of bombs we'd drop, sometimes we carried napalm where you saw a path of fire destruction, or we carried these parafragmentation bombs, which we dropped them in sequence, okay? And they had a little drag chute on the bomb, and that would give us some time to get away because we were just down at treetop level. So we could get away from that, and a whole string of bombs would come right down.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Did you have much antiaircraft fire then?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, it wasn't the--well, it was the antiaircraft, but we were so low it was ground fire. You never saw--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Until you passed.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: --until you got shot up. You never saw it. With all fairness, we got shot, you know. When we went over to a target, we went over as a squadron of 12 planes and then we'd break off and we all do our own thing. When we were done, we wouldn't regroup. We'd justgo back to the base.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: You ever run into any enemy aircraft?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No. We had--I think we had the supremacy of the air at that time when I was over, you know.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: What year was this?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I went over in--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: This is '44?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: '44. Four of '44.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: And you're now primarily in the lower Philippines.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Most of our missions were in the Philippines. We had--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Had Leyte Island been taken then?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Which island?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Leyte.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Leyte, we took Leyte.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We took Leyte, and then we landed at Leyte, and my whole--the whole group went up by LST to carry all of our equipment. We flew up and we based at Leyte, and then we were flying out of Leyte, okay?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Is that Tacloban?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: What camp?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Tacloban, the airfield at Leyte.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I don't remember the name of an airfield. We didn't use names, did we? But anyway, we flew missions out of there. And then I moved up to another island called Mindoro.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Yeah, that was south.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: South of Luzon. South of the main island of Luzon. It was further north of Leyte. And we were there for a good period of time, and we were flying all over Luzon. We bombed Clark Field. That was, oh, that was a big raid. We had maybe about 500 sorties flying that day. And we were just down there strafing the hell out of those Japanese planes on the ground. Don't forget, we're treetop level, we're flying right down there. And shooting up and everything, like--you know. And by the way, we had one mission over Corregidor, and it was a joint venture between the Navy and the Air Corps, and the Navy were lobbing shells into the island of Corregidor, and when they got through, we went in. You know how many passes we made over that island? We made seven passes all because we still had ammo, and Junior was just like, "You got any ammo left? Yeah. Okay, let's go, one more time." Seven passes over there until we ran out of ammo. And that was a thrilling mission. Another mission was a shipping mission. And that's tough. It was supply ships. You know, they were armed and everything like that.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: They were out on the sea or in the harbor?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: At sea. At sea. And that was the worst mission I was on. But thank God we made it back. You know, concentrated fire power. And there's Junior doing all kinds of evasive action until we got close to the target and he'd deh-deh-deh, and we'd bank up and I'd give off my burst, you know? And that was the worst mission.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: What was that ship that you were attacking? That was not alone, was it?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No, it was a fleet of ships. Yeah, a group of ships, supply ships.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So they were escorted by enemy--

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: --men of war?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We were picking at supply ships. By the way, at Mindoro there was one situation there where the Japs had a fleet of ships that were trying to take back that island that we were situated on, okay? So they got us together and said we'd have to dig in because the Japs want to take this island. A whole bunch of ships coming down towards Mindoro. So we got our foxhole and we got in, put our guns and everything in it expecting the worst. But what happened all night long we had our night fighters taking off, constantly going out and hitting that whole fleet of ships until we destroyed a good part of them, and they turned around and went back, thank God. That was at Mindoro, okay? And other missions would stand out in my mind, some peculiar missions.There was one mission that we were flying down--we had broken off and we were doing our strafing and everything, and we were coming down a dirt road, and there's a Japanese command car coming right down the road. Okay? And Junior starts strafing with his four 50s, and actually, I'm over the top and I can see, and the doors fly open and they all start taking off, and I said, "Junior, bank," and as he banked (motioning machine gun shooting.) That was funny. But...

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So you were flying a lot of missions.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I flew 22 missions, okay?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: This was primarily the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yes, that's all. But before the war ended in August, okay, prior to that time you get rotated back to the States, they had a point system where they gave you points for so many hours in the air and points if you were shot up, okay? So we were flying short-range missions, two hours, three hours because we was always up on the front line. So I says at this rate I'll never get home, you know. So I transferred into a B-24 Bomb Group. It was called the Jolly Rogers.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: This is still in the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yes. Yes. It was on an island in the Philippines. Not in the main island.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Had the war ended yet?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No, no. This was all just before the war ended. Because I wanted to get more points, and with the B-24s they were in the air nine, 10 hours, you know, and flak and everything, they get shot up. You know, you get a lot of points. And I joined this group, and it was the Jolly Rogers. Did you ever hear of that, the skull and cross bones on the tail? Well, I joined that group, and I flew one exciting mission. We took off from our base and we landed at Okinawa and we stayed overnight. They armed us with our bombs and everything like that. Then we took off and we bombed Shanghai, China, okay? That was the last mission I was on. Then the war was over when they dropped the A-bomb.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: How did you feel when you heard the A-bomb was dropped?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: How did I feel? I feel good. Because if they didn't drop that bomb, I may not be here talking to you. And not only that, it saved a lot of lives. I know a lot of people were against that. "How could you do that? The women and children." But it ended the war. Can you imagine if we had to invade Tokyo? We were right there. I was on Ryukyu Islands at that time. An island that was called Ie Shima. That's where Ernie Pyle was killed by a Japanese bullet, by the way.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That was off Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah. And we were right off Tokyo Bay. I mean, the next step would have been the island of Japan. Can you imagine the havoc? Because these Japanese were fanatic fighters. And we would have lost a lot. And I was in favor of it. A lot of people say hey...

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So they dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We dropped the A-bomb.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: The war was over. And you're lookingto gather up all the points you can get to get back home.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, it was different. The war was over. There weren't any more points. So we were just waiting to come back to the States.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Before you get back to the States, you have a couple of pictures. Would you like to explain them? I'll hold them up.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, that is a picture of the Japanese surrender party that landed on the island of Ie Shima, okay? And you can see what a sullen, defeated group of officers that they were. Look at them. No conversation between them. Just a note of defeat. The invincible Japanese Empire in defeat. They're waiting to be taken over to the Battleship Missouri to sign a Peace Treaty. You know why it was the Battleship Missouri and not the Battleship New Jersey? Do you know why?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Because Truman was president. He was from Missouri.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I'll tell you something. You have another picture. You want to hold that up, Jonathan?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's another group, the same situation, okay? And you can see the plane they flew in that the rising sun was painted over and they put a red cross on it. It's hard to make that out really. Oh, you can see it. I can see it here. Yeah. And this is the island of Ie Shima, the surrender party waiting to be taken over to the Battleship Missouri to sign a Peace Treaty with General MacArthur. And his famous words when he was--they knocked him out of the Pacific, "I shall return." He returned. We returned. And here goes the Empire of Japan.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Now, you have a booklet here. Anything special you want to say about this? We're not going to be able to show every page.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: No, I'm not going to show every page.I just want to tell you that we did this book when the war was ongoing, and I just want to show you one picture of our CO that was shot down, okay? Colonel Elmore. But anyway, he was shot down, and we were heartbroken when he went in. You know, you never see these guys go down, you know? That's Johnson. But anyway...

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That had to be a very hard time for you when the war was over. (Jonathan hands Mr. Ciccone a picture.)

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Oh, here it is, yeah, excuse me.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Go ahead. You can hold that, Jonathan.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's Colonel Elmore. He never cameback. He was in charge of the whole bomb group, okay?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: He looked like he was a young man.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: We were all young. We were kids fighting the war. All the old people were sitting back and telling us what to do; is that right?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: All right now. Look at this. You got to see this. Now, this is--you can hold them up, okay? This is the honor roll. These are all the guys that didn't make it, that never came back. Now, don't forget now, the whole group consisted of a lot of people. But this is the combat crew. For every person that was in combat, there may have been maybe a dozen, 15 people on the ground to take care of everything else. These are the guys that never came back. I can tell you incidents of one guy, his name sticks out in my mind, Ronzoni, first mission, first blood, never came back. Then it was another staff sergeant that he needed one more mission to get an Air Medal, never came back. Now, one of my friends had the GI or dysentery. One day he didn't go on the flight, his plane didn't come back.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Speaking of awards, how many awards and citations did your captain award you?Do you recall what medals you earned, ribbons?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Can I show that?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: By all means. That's why I'm asking the question.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: All right. And actually, these here--I'll point to these--these are commendations, all right? And we were commendated for various actions that we took. And I took them out of this book that we made up.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: You want to explain the ribbons?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: The ribbons--I'll get my discharge papers here, I'll show you. It'll explain what, you know...

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I see the American Theater there. Asiatic Pacific, the Victory Medal.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's right. And the Philippines Liberation Medal, the American Service Ribbon, Asiatic Pacific. And I had four stars on the Asiatic Pacific. That was China, Luzon, New Guinea, and the southern Philippines. Those are stars on this medal here, okay? And all of these were taken from this book, and I put that together after the war.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Who's that young man there that looksso handsome?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Somebody told me they recognized thatpicture by my eyebrows.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That looks like when you were born you're so young.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I was 18.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: And you see this here? That was from that hat. It's still here. 67 years old.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So now when you finally got enough points to be sent home, when did that happen?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I never got enough points. I never got enough points because the war was over.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So how long before they sent you back to the States?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you, I was on that island Ie Shima, it was about five-by-seven miles, and every day I'd get up on the highest part of that terrain there and with binoculars I would look out for a ship, and it was four months before they finally came and got us. Four months sitting there. And we got back on the Liberty Ship.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: While you're flying to and from Ie Shima, did you happen to look down and notice how many damaged American destroyers and ships there were laying around by the island?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I didn't see any of that. You know, because we flew so low and everything, you know. Even coming back in from the mission we'd be treetop level. One time I was shot up and the right engine was smoking on this plane there, and it was smoking, and I told Junior, Well--actually, I wore a chest harness. I couldn't wear a chute. We didn't have enough room, and in case I had to jump, I had a chute which would hook right onto the harness. When I saw that engine smoking like that, I said, "Hey Junior, if I see fire, I'm going, I'm leaving." And thank God that we got back to the base. And what had happened, a couple of cylinders had misfired from a shot or something like that, and all it was doing was exhausting unspent fuel, you know? And that's really--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So when did you finally hit the States?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Get back to the States? In December--

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: '45, right. What a welcome we got. San Francis--

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Did you go back to the East Coast?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's where I got discharged, but wespent quite a bit of time in Frisco. We got all kinds of welcoming parties. All groups, you know, giving us dinners and everything like that. And the fire boats as we came into the harbor under the Golden Gate, and they were just streaming water out, and we were so happy. And I hadn't seen a female in three years, you know that. End that.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Was there any one event or person that still stands out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Any one event. During that war. Well, I think when we lost our CO, that stood out in my mind.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Well, that had to be a harrowing experience.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Yeah, it was something. And you know, they would post our mission the day before. Anybody who said they weren't scared when they saw they were flying the next day is full of baloney. And by the way, in East Indies, we were close to Australia, we would send out, we'd call it a fat cat plane to go to Australia and load up with booze and everything like that, and they would come back and we'd have a good time. You know how we cooled our beer? Ingenuity. We'd get a hot--hundred octane gasoline, put it into a can, put a pin hole in it, let it drip on the beer. Hundred octane evaporates like that. It would cool the beer.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: That's something. I never heard of that. That sounds...

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Well, there you go, kid.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Vince, I want to thank you very much for coming in here and sharing your story with us. I'm sorry, you have something else?

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I have my jacket. You want to see that? My A-2 flying jacket? You can lift the plastic on it. This is an A-2 flying jacket. Government issue, okay? What I did, I decorated that. What I did was, I went to a sports store and I took the insignias from this book here and I had them with their computers they made copies and they did it up like that. And there's the 5th Air Force. Turn it around. You see my squadron, 675th Squadron, the Dauntless Demons, right? That's it. There's my original wings and my--you see the wings up there? They're kind of tarnished. I should clean 'em, right? You see there's a bullet with wings on it there? That's my original wings, okay? A-2 flying jacket.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Thank you. Again, thank you for sharing your stories with us.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: I wish I could tell you more.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: You told us quite a bit. You were coming fast and lucid. You did an outstanding job. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay. Thank you, Paul. It's nice tobe here and I wish I could talk for another hour really.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Now, when you were flying, making these missions over Japan, if you had looked down and you saw some destroyers around, that would have been my ship, one of them there. We were out off the coast of Japan when the war ended.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, we sailed right into Tokyo Bay.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: That's after the war was over.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: We went into Tokyo Bay, anchored right near the Missouri when they were signing the Peace Treaty.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: So I know where you're coming from.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Ie Shima, that's where we were. And actually, right after the war was over,we did no more bombing really.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: I know. Thank you again.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Thank you. Nice to be here.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Thank you, Jonathan.

sp.speaker: Vincent Ciccone
sp.p: Okay. Now we'll wrap it up.

sp.speaker: Paul Frisco
sp.p: Now you're free to go. (Interview concludes.)
